concept.name: Alternative hypothesis
concept.definition: The claim about the population that contradicts the null hypothesis - typically what the researcher suspects or hopes to demonstrate - and the conclusion adopted when the null is rejected. It never contains an equality, taking forms mu != mu_0, mu > mu_0, or mu < mu_0.
concept.intuition: It is the contender: 'this strategy does have an edge.' You get to assert it only by showing the data are inconsistent with the null.
concept.mechanics: The choice of alternative determines the rejection region: a two-sided Ha (mu != mu_0) splits alpha into both tails, while one-sided alternatives (mu > mu_0 or mu < mu_0) place the entire critical region in one tail, changing the critical value and the power against effects in that direction.
concept.formula: Forms: Ha: mu != mu_0 with rejection region |T| > t_{1-alpha/2}; Ha: mu > mu_0 with T > t_{1-alpha}; Ha: mu < mu_0 with T < t_{alpha}, where T is the test statistic and t the appropriate t-distribution critical value.
concept.failure_modes: Choosing the alternative after seeing the data (deciding on a one-sided test because the sign is known) invalidates the stated error rates. A test is only powerful against alternatives in the direction specified, so a wrong-sided or overly narrow Ha can fail to detect a real effect.
concept.misconceptions: Rejecting H0 does not prove Ha is true or economically important - it only means the data are sufficiently inconsistent with H0. Nor may the alternative contain an equality; by convention the equality always belongs to the null.
concept.example: For a mean-reversion signal the analyst sets H0: mu >= 0 against Ha: mu < 0 (expected negative mean spread change); a one-sided rejection region in the left tail concentrates all power on detecting the predicted direction.
